To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) HPWS practices have a positive effect on employee outcomes, (b) this effect is partially mediated by the degree to which employees perceive their work as orderly and predictable, (c) the effect of HPWS practices on employee outcomes is moderated by the industry in which employees work and (d) the effect of the HPWS practices on the degree of employee order and predictability is moderated by employees’ age and gender.
HPWS practices are positively associated with employee perceptions of workplace order and predict-ability and that these associations are mediated by perceptions of workplace order.
HPWS practices contribute significantly and positively to workplace order and that the positive outcomes associated with HPWS practices are mediated by order.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between work systems and employee outcomes.
the effects of ‘high performance work practices’, which we define as the set of work practices that are intended to improve the performance of an organisation.
the effects of ‘high performance work systems’ on the experiences of employees in the Australian aged care sector.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the HPWS practices in question, when implemented in the context of an industry and employee group with a history of high levels of employee commitment and engagement, can be expected to have positive effects on employee outcomes.
the HPWS practices are not necessarily bad for workers.
HPWS practices are associated with employee experience of order and predictabiltiy in the aged care industry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results of the study suggest that HPWS practices contribute significantly to the experience of order and predictabiliy in the workplace, and that these in turn contribute to positive outcomes for employees.
HPWS practices can be beneficial for employees in terms of their experience of work.
we have shown how HPWS practices can be understood in terms of the interests of both capital and labour.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HPWS literature would be better served by considering how HPWS practices contribute, not just to the interests of employers, but also to the interests of workers.
HPWS practices are not necessarily bad for workers, as they can contribute to a sense of order and predictablity in the workplace.
the HPWS literature would benefit from greater attention to contextual factors and the role of interests in shaping employee responses to HPWS.
